questions.prompt: Which combination is a classic phishing sign?

options.text: Urgent pressure plus a shortened link
A message that uses your correct first name only
options.explanationWrong: A name alone proves nothing. Scammers can find names easily.

options.text: A message with no link at all
options.explanationWrong: Scams can also ask you to call or reply, so no link is not proof of safety.

options.text: A message sent during the day
options.explanationWrong: Scammers send messages at any time.

questions.explanationCorrect: Pressure plus a link that hides its destination is a classic warning. Slow down and check.

questions.prompt: A message asks for your OTP 'to verify'. What do you do?

options.text: Share it, since it is only a few digits
options.explanationWrong: An OTP can approve a payment or login. Never share it.

options.text: Share it only if the message looks official
options.explanationWrong: Official looks are easy to copy.

options.text: Never share it, and contact the organisation through its official app or helpline
Reply asking why they need it
options.explanationWrong: Replying tells the scammer you are active. Do not engage.

questions.explanationCorrect: Never share an OTP. Check with the organisation using its official app or helpline.

questions.prompt: A link in an SMS looks odd. What is the best action?

options.text: Tap it to see where it goes
options.explanationWrong: Tapping can open a fake page. Avoid it.
That spreads the risk. Do not forward suspicious links.

options.text: Open it on a different phone
options.explanationWrong: The link is still unsafe on any device.

options.text: Do not tap it. Open the official app yourself

questions.explanationCorrect: Skip the link. Open the official app yourself and check there.
